html:
In 204 BCE Rome brought the sacred stone of the Great Mother, the Anatolian goddess Cybele, from Asia Minor to the city, hoping she would help it defeat Hannibal.

After years of the Second Punic War, and a series of bad omens, the Senate consulted the Sibylline Books, Rome's books of prophecy. They said a foreign invader could be driven out if the Idaean Mother were brought to Rome. With the help of King Attalus I of Pergamon, the Romans fetched her holy object, a black stone, from her shrine at Pessinus. A young noble judged the best man in Rome received it at the coast. Legend says that when the ship stuck in the Tiber, a noblewoman named Claudia Quinta pulled it free to prove her virtue.

Hannibal left Italy the next year. The goddess got a temple on the Palatine and yearly games. But her rites, led by eunuch priests called Galli, shocked the Romans, and for a long time citizens were barred from her priesthood. Rome welcomed foreign gods on its own terms, as the later ban on the Bacchanalia showed.
sum: In 204 BCE Rome brought the sacred stone of the Great Mother, the Anatolian goddess Cybele, from Asia Minor to the city, hoping she would help it defeat Hannibal.
